request.explanation: a wish for the contact to stop when signs such as tail lashing, skin twitching, ears back or a direct stare appear (petting-induced aggression may follow)

uncertainty: The recording can show what the animal does and when; it cannot establish why. Candidate explanations come from the cited sources, ordered by how well your description matches them.
Behaviour recognition uses a general vision-language model (zero-shot); scores are relative, not probabilities, and its measured accuracy is in results/e31.
No usable sound in the recording, so vocalizations could not be checked.
Context taken from the recording (people, objects, sounds, place) comes from automatic detectors and can be wrong; it changes the order of the candidates only half as much as your description.
observations_needed: Is it frequent or focused on one place (ears, neck)?
Are there fleas, flea dirt, redness or discharge from the ears?
Was a plant, a catnip toy or a new object nearby?
Does the cat also lick or chew the object?
Where is the cat touched when it reacts, and what does its tail and ears do just before?
Does it seek contact again afterwards?
urgent_signs: bleeding or open sores from scratching
sudden new sensitivity to touch at one place (possible pain)

sources.supports: itch is the most common sign of skin disease and leads to scratching, licking and biting; behavioural causes link to stress, frustration or conflict; diagnosis of exclusion

sources.citation: Waisglass SE et al. (2006) Underlying medical conditions in cats with presumptive psychogenic alopecia. J Am Vet Med Assoc 228(11):1705-1709.
sources.supports: of 21 overgrooming cats presumed psychogenic, 16 had a medical cause of itch, 3 both, 2 a purely behavioural cause

sources.citation: Bol S et al. (2017) Responsiveness of cats to silver vine, Tatarian honeysuckle, valerian and catnip. BMC Vet Res 13:70.
sources.supports: nearly all of 100 domestic cats responded to at least one plant; one in three did not respond to catnip, almost 80 % responded to silver vine

sources.citation: Cornell Feline Health Center: Feline behavior problems: aggression.
sources.supports: petting-induced aggression (over-stimulation, the cat controlling when petting ends) is often preceded by dilated pupils, tail lashing and ears moved back; a relaxed cat holds its tail up with no flicking or twitching; seeing an outdoor cat through a window can trigger redirected aggression; cats in pain may act aggressively to avoid touch

sources.citation: Animal Humane Society: Petting-induced and play aggression in cats.
sources.supports: tail lashing or thumping, shifting body position, skin twitching and direct stares indicate the cat has had enough petting

sources.citation: Kim SA (2025) Behavior problems of cats. Merck Veterinary Manual.
sources.supports: petting-induced aggression from low tolerance of contact or over-stimulation; arousal can be redirected; some cats use threatening displays to remove a fear-evoking stimulus; medical problems must be ruled out before a problem is called behavioural

answer.summary: In the recording: being touched or stroked by a person (0.0-20.0 s). Movement: the animal stays roughly in place while moving. Scratching its own body with a hind foot (user report only) has several possible explanations, in order of fit to your description: discomfort, itch, pain or a neurological cause; ordinary play or maintenance behaviour. No request is implied by it. Rolling on the back or rubbing the face or body on objects (user report only) is usually ordinary play or maintenance behaviour. No request is implied by it. The cause is not established from the recording; the questions listed would help tell the candidates apart.
